options: Starting with k clusters and merging until one remains
Starting with each observation in its own cluster and merging bottom-up
Randomly assigning observations and then computing centroids
questions.explanation: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with n singletons and merges the two closest clusters at each step, building up the dendrogram from the bottom. Divisive clustering (DIANA) goes top-down.

options: The maximum pairwise distance between clusters
The minimum pairwise distance between clusters
The increase in total within-cluster variance when merging two clusters
The average pairwise distance between all observations
questions.explanation: Ward.D2 merges the pair of clusters whose fusion produces the smallest increase in total within-cluster variance (sum of squared deviations). This tends to produce compact, equal-sized clusters.

questions.text: Hierarchical clustering is generally faster than k-means for datasets with 100,000+ observations.
questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering requires computing an n × n distance matrix, which is O(n²) in memory and O(n² log n) in time. For large n this becomes infeasible. k-Means is O(nkd) per iteration and scales much better.

questions.text: What is the purpose of cutree(hc, k = 4)?
options: Prunes branches of the dendrogram below height 4
Returns cluster labels by cutting the dendrogram at a level that yields 4 clusters
Runs hierarchical clustering with k = 4 initial clusters
Removes 4 outlier observations from the clustering
questions.explanation: cutree() converts the hierarchical tree to a flat partition. Specifying k = 4 cuts at the height where exactly 4 clusters are obtained. You can also specify h (height) instead of k.

questions.text: Which linkage method is most prone to 'chaining' (producing long, elongated clusters)?
questions.explanation: Single linkage uses the minimum pairwise distance between clusters. A new observation only needs to be close to the nearest point in a cluster to be merged into it, creating chains of loosely connected points.
